questions.stem: An emergency department uses the 5-level Emergency Severity Index (ESI). For each arriving client, indicate the triage level.

rows.text: A 58-year-old who is unresponsive with agonal breathing
A 64-year-old with crushing chest pain for 20 minutes and normal vital signs
A 30-year-old with abdominal pain and vomiting who needs labs, IV fluids and a CT
A 22-year-old with an ankle injury who can walk and needs only an x-ray

columns.text: ESI 3 (stable, needs two or more resources)

rationale.correct: ESI: level 1 needs life-saving action now; level 2 is high risk or confused, lethargic or in severe pain; levels 3 to 5 are sorted by the number of resources needed.

perOption.r2:c1: Does not need an immediate life-saving procedure yet.
perOption.r2:c2: High-risk chest pain should not wait.
perOption.r3:c2: Not high-risk based on the data.

references: NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan
NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: On Monday morning, a home health nurse reviews voicemails and plans a route for four scheduled visits across the county. Which client should the nurse go to first?

options.text: A client with diabetes who needs a weekly insulin pen review and a full foot check
A client after hip surgery with new calf pain and swelling
A client with COPD who needs a monthly oxygen equipment and safety review
A client with a stage 2 pressure injury that needs its scheduled dressing change

rationale.correct: In home health, visit first the client with signs of a new, possibly life-threatening complication; schedule routine visits after.

perOption.a: A routine teaching visit can be scheduled later.
perOption.b: New calf pain and swelling after hip surgery suggest a DVT, which can lead to pulmonary embolism.
perOption.c: A routine equipment check can wait.
perOption.d: Scheduled wound care is less urgent than a possible DVT.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: In a long-term care facility, the RN is making assignments. Which 2 tasks should the RN assign to the LPN?

options.text: Giving scheduled medications through an established gastrostomy tube
Assessing a resident who has a new change in mental status
Changing a dressing on a healing stage 2 pressure injury
Developing a new care plan for a resident admitted today
Evaluating whether a resident's new antidepressant is working

rationale.correct: Assign LPNs medications and treatments for stable residents; keep new assessments, care planning and evaluation of new therapies.

perOption.a: Within LPN scope for stable residents.
perOption.b: A new change needs RN assessment.
perOption.c: Routine wound care is within LPN scope.
perOption.d: Care planning is an RN responsibility.
perOption.e: Evaluating response to a new therapy needs RN judgment.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Assign tasks to an LPN in long-term care.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a situation with a new graduate: a client in severe pain asks for an extra opioid dose that is not prescribed, and the nurse instead calls the provider for a pain plan change. Complete the sentences.

content.template: By not giving an unprescribed dose that could cause respiratory depression, the nurse is upholding {{b1}}. By pursuing better pain relief through the provider, the nurse is upholding {{b2}}.

options.text: nonmaleficence
justice
veracity
beneficence
autonomy
fidelity

rationale.correct: Nonmaleficence means avoiding harm; beneficence means acting for the client's good. Nurses often balance both.

perOption.b2:a: Acting to benefit the client is beneficence.
perOption.b2:b: Autonomy is respecting the client's choices.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client received a tenfold overdose of IV morphine because of a pump programming error and needed naloxone. The client has recovered. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continue to monitor the client's breathing and sedation closely
Notify the provider about the error and the client's condition
Take part in honest disclosure of the error to the client as policy directs
Write "incident report completed" in the client's record
Complete an incident report through the safety system
Ask the pharmacy to change the record so the dose appears correct

rationale.correct: After an error that reaches the client: care for and monitor the client, notify the provider, disclose honestly per policy and report through the safety system without altering or referencing it in the record.

perOption.a: Monitoring continues while the opioid wears off.
perOption.c: Clients have a right to know about errors that affect them.
perOption.d: The incident report is not mentioned in the record.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a medication error that caused harm.

questions.stem: A client who fell yesterday asks the nurse for a copy of the incident report about the fall. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "I'll print you a copy now, since the report is about your own care."
"That report is internal, but you can request your health record."
"There is no report, so there's nothing to give you."
"You'll need to hire a lawyer to see anything about the fall."

rationale.correct: Incident reports are confidential quality documents; clients can see the facts in their own health record.

perOption.a: Incident reports are internal quality documents, not part of the health record.
perOption.b: The client can request their health record, which includes the facts of the fall.
perOption.d: Clients can access their own health records without a lawyer.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a request for an incident report.

questions.stem: A nurse manager is reviewing conflict-resolution strategies. For each situation, choose the strategy being used.

cells.text: Two nurses who both want the same holiday off work out a plan in which each gets half the day
The manager ignores ongoing tension between two staff members, hoping it will settle
The team works together to design a new break schedule that meets everyone's needs
A nurse agrees to the charge nurse's plan just to keep the peace, though they disagree

options.text: Compromise
Avoidance
Competition
Collaboration
Avoidance
Compromise
Collaboration
Accommodation
Avoidance
Competition
Collaboration
Accommodation

rationale.correct: Conflict strategies: collaboration (win-win), compromise (each gives some), accommodation (giving in), avoidance (ignoring) and competition (forcing).

perOption.b3:a: Working together for a solution that meets all needs is collaboration.
perOption.b4:a: The nurse did not push their view.
perOption.b4:c: Giving in to keep the peace is accommodation.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's family member approaches the nurse, upset that call lights were not answered promptly overnight. Place the nurse's actions in order.

items.text: Follow up with the family member about what was found and changed
Look into what happened and involve the charge nurse or manager
Listen without interrupting and acknowledge the family member's concern
Apologize for the experience and explain what the nurse will do

rationale.correct: Handling complaints: listen, acknowledge and apologize, investigate with leadership, then follow up.

perOption.b: An apology and a plan build trust.
perOption.d: Closing the loop shows the concern was taken seriously.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a complaint about care.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia leaves against medical advice. Review the nurse's draft note and highlight the parts that are appropriate and important to document.

segments.text: The provider explained the risks of leaving, including worsening infection and death
The client repeated the risks back in their own words
The client was being difficult and rude to staff
The client signed the against-medical-advice form
The nurse removed the IV catheter intact and gave written follow-up instructions
The nurse thinks the client will be back by tomorrow

rationale.correct: AMA documentation: risks explained by the provider, the client's understanding, the signed form, care given at departure and follow-up instructions; no opinions.

perOption.s1: Documenting that risks were explained is essential.
perOption.s5: Subjective, judgmental statements do not belong in the record.
perOption.s7: The signed form or a refusal to sign is documented.
perOption.s11: Speculation does not belong in the record.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Document a discharge against medical advice.

questions.stem: A client's employer calls the unit asking whether the client will be able to return to work next week and what the diagnosis is. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Share the expected return date but not the diagnosis
Say that nothing can be shared without the client's written consent
Give the information, since employers need it to plan staffing
Transfer the employer to the client's room so the employer can ask the client directly

rationale.correct: Employers receive health information only with the client's written authorization.

perOption.a: Even return-to-work information needs the client's permission.
perOption.b: Employers are not entitled to health information without the client's authorization.
perOption.c: Business needs do not override privacy.
perOption.d: Connecting the call confirms the client is there and may pressure the client.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's insurer denies payment for another hospital day, but the nurse believes the client still needs inpatient care because of unstable oxygen levels. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Discharge the client, since the insurer will not pay for another day
Document the findings and work with the case manager on an appeal
Tell the client to pay for the extra day personally
Keep the client in the hospital without telling anyone about the insurer's denial

rationale.correct: Case managers handle utilization review; nurses support appeals with clear documentation of clinical need.

perOption.a: Payment decisions do not override clinical need.
perOption.b: Clear documentation and case management support an appeal or a safe alternative plan.
perOption.c: This shifts the problem without addressing clinical need or appeals.
perOption.d: The team must address the denial openly.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: For each client need after discharge, indicate the most appropriate community resource.

rows.text: A homebound older adult who cannot shop or cook
A client with dementia whose spouse works during the day
A client with end-stage cancer who chooses comfort care at home
A client going home with IV antibiotics through a PICC

rationale.correct: Match needs to resources: meals for nutrition, day programs for supervision and respite, hospice for end-of-life care and home health for skilled nursing.

perOption.r2:c2: Supervised day programs give care and respite.
perOption.r4:c4: Home health provides skilled IV care.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A unit has a provider-approved hypoglycemia protocol. A client's fingerstick glucose is 58 mg/dL, and the client is alert and can swallow. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Call the provider and wait for a prescription before treating
Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate per protocol and recheck
Give IV 50% dextrose, since that works faster than oral treatment
Hold the next insulin dose and recheck the client's glucose before dinner tonight

rationale.correct: Nurses may act under approved protocols and standing orders within their defined limits, then notify and document as required.

perOption.a: The protocol allows prompt treatment; waiting delays care.
perOption.b: Approved protocols let nurses act within defined limits without waiting for individual orders.
perOption.c: IV dextrose is for clients who cannot swallow; the protocol uses oral treatment first.
perOption.d: This does not treat the current low glucose.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A unit is reducing medication errors. For each area, select the practices that reduce errors.

options.text: Prepare medications in a quiet zone without interruptions
Prepare several clients' medications at once to save time
Check the label against the record three times
Scan the client's wristband and the medication barcode
Leave the medications at the bedside for the client to take later
Explain each medication to the client before giving it

rationale.correct: Reduce medication errors with no-interruption zones, label checks, barcode scanning and client involvement.

perOption.a: Interruptions are a major cause of errors.
perOption.e: The nurse cannot confirm the dose was taken.
perOption.f: Clients often catch errors when they know what to expect.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: Two residents in a long-term care facility tell the charge nurse that an assistive personnel (AP) has been rough and impatient during care. What should the charge nurse do first?

options.text: Move the AP to a different hall so the residents feel safer
Keep residents safe, then report and investigate per policy
Ask the AP to apologize to the residents and be more gentle
Wait to see whether more residents complain about the AP before acting

rationale.correct: Allegations of resident mistreatment require immediate protection, reporting and investigation according to facility policy and law.

perOption.a: Moving the AP does not investigate or protect other residents.
perOption.b: Possible mistreatment requires protecting residents and reporting according to policy and law.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A client is invited to join a clinical trial of a new heart failure drug. Which rights should the nurse make sure the client understands? Select all that apply.

options.text: The client can refuse to join without affecting their usual care
The client can withdraw from the study at any time
The client's information will be kept confidential
The client must stay in the study until it ends once they sign
The client should be told the risks and possible benefits

rationale.correct: Research participants have the right to informed consent, voluntary participation, withdrawal at any time and confidentiality.

perOption.d: Clients can leave at any time.
perOption.e: Informed consent includes risks and benefits.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: Which event is considered a sentinel event that requires a root cause analysis?

options.text: A client misses a scheduled walk in the hallway because of a busy shift
A client dies after an unnoticed drop in oxygen on a PCA
A client refuses a dose of a stool softener
A client's meal tray arrives 20 minutes late

rationale.correct: Sentinel events are unexpected occurrences causing death or serious harm; they require a root cause analysis.

perOption.b: An unexpected death or serious harm related to care is a sentinel event.
perOption.c: A refusal is not an event.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A power outage hits the hospital, and the backup generator fails on one wing for several minutes. Which client should the nurse check first?

options.text: A client on a continuous IV infusion pump that has a battery backup
A client on a mechanical ventilator whose battery alarm is sounding
A client receiving oxygen at 2 L/min from a wall outlet
A client with a bed alarm that turned off

rationale.correct: During power failure, check life-support equipment first and be ready to ventilate manually with a bag-valve mask.

perOption.a: Pumps with batteries continue to run.
perOption.b: A ventilator-dependent client may need manual ventilation with a bag-valve mask if power is lost.
perOption.c: Piped oxygen does not depend on electricity.
perOption.d: Fall risk matters, but a ventilator-dependent client is at greater immediate risk.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A nurse is doing a scheduled telehealth video visit with a client at home. Which action best protects the client's privacy?

options.text: Use the secure telehealth platform from a private room
Use a personal video app on the nurse's own phone for convenience
Do the visit from the open nurses' station so others can help
Record the visit and share it with coworkers for teaching

rationale.correct: Telehealth privacy: secure platforms, private settings, verified identity and no unconsented recording.

perOption.a: Secure platforms and a private setting protect confidential information.
perOption.b: Personal apps may not be secure.
perOption.d: Recording and sharing without consent breaches privacy.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: Ten minutes after a urinary catheter is inserted, a client with spina bifida and a history of reactions to balloons develops hives, wheezing and swelling of the lips. Blood pressure falls from 118/72 to 82/48 mm Hg. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Remove the latex catheter and call for help
Give oral diphenhydramine and recheck in an hour
Replace the catheter with another one from the same supply
Sit the client fully upright with the legs down

parameters.text: Color and clarity of the urine in the bag
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants

rationale.correct: Latex anaphylaxis: remove the source, give epinephrine, support airway and circulation and use latex-free equipment.

perOption.c1: Hives, wheezing, lip swelling and hypotension after contact with a latex catheter in a client at high risk show latex anaphylaxis.
perOption.c2: Infection does not cause sudden hives and wheezing.
perOption.c3: Vasovagal reactions cause a slow pulse without hives or wheezing.
perOption.c4: Asthma does not cause hives and lip swelling.
perOption.a1: Removing the trigger stops further exposure.
perOption.a4: The same supply may contain latex.
perOption.a5: Hypotension is treated with the client lying with legs raised unless breathing requires otherwise.
perOption.p1: Show response to treatment of shock.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: On a busy medical unit, an infection prevention nurse reviews four newly admitted clients whose diagnoses are confirmed and teaches staff which precautions each one needs. For each condition, select every type of transmission-based precaution the nurse should use.

rows.text: Disseminated herpes zoster in an immunocompromised client
Meningococcal meningitis in the first 24 hours of treatment

rationale.correct: Some conditions need more than one type of precaution; disseminated zoster needs contact and airborne precautions.

perOption.r1:c3: Disseminated zoster can spread through the air.

questions.stem: The nurse audits the record of a client in soft wrist restraints. Highlight the findings that do not meet restraint standards.

cells: Written as "restraints as needed" with no time limit

rationale.correct: Restraint records need a time-limited order, documented alternatives, regular checks of circulation and skin, and care for fluids, nutrition and toileting.

perOption.r1: As-needed restraint orders are not allowed; orders must be time-limited.
perOption.r3: Less restrictive alternatives must be tried and documented.
perOption.r5: Basic needs must be met and documented.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client who received oral radioactive iodine (I-131) 6 hours ago vomits on the floor of the private room. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Clean the vomit right away with paper towels and put them in the regular trash
Keep others out, contain it with PPE and call radiation safety
Leave the vomit until the next day so the radioactivity can decay
Move the client to a shared room down the hall while the floor is cleaned

rationale.correct: After radioactive iodine, body fluids are contaminated; contain spills with PPE, limit access and follow radiation safety procedures.

perOption.a: Vomit is radioactive; it needs radiation safety procedures.
perOption.b: Body fluids after I-131 are radioactive; the area is secured and radiation safety directs the cleanup.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching the family of a client with moderate dementia who lives at home. Which safety measures should the nurse recommend? Select all that apply.

options.text: Install locks or alarms on doors that lead outside
Remove knobs from the stove or use an automatic shutoff
Keep medications in a locked container and give them to the client
Rearrange the furniture often to keep the brain active
Use night lights in the hallway and bathroom
Leave car keys where the client can find them to keep independence
Lower the water heater temperature to prevent burns

rationale.correct: Home safety in dementia: secure exits, stove safety, locked medications, consistent layout, night lights and no driving.

perOption.f: Driving with moderate dementia is unsafe.
perOption.g: People with dementia may not sense or react to hot water.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: An overhead announcement reports an active shooter on the floor below the nurse's unit. Clients cannot be safely moved out of the building. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Go to the floor below to help any injured people
Lock or barricade doors, silence phones and hide clients
Gather the clients in the hallway so that they can be counted quickly
Call each family to let them know about the situation

rationale.correct: Active threat: run if a safe exit exists, otherwise hide (lock, barricade, silence) and fight only as a last resort; protect clients who cannot move.

perOption.a: Moving toward the threat endangers staff and clients.
perOption.b: If evacuation is not safe, hiding and barricading is the recommended response.
perOption.c: Gathering in the hallway exposes clients.
perOption.d: Phone calls draw attention and are not the priority.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
